scenarios.title: A join before auth.success is refused without a request, and the join after it binds to the connection id with a fresh admission and resume token
scenarios.why: The server binds a participation only to the socket named by connectionId, which the controller learns from auth.success.

scenarios.title: When a join's reply is lost, the same join on the same socket sends the same admission id and resume token
scenarios.why: The server may have admitted the first request; it answers a repeated admissionId with its first answer only when the request is the same.

scenarios.title: Re-authenticating the same socket keeps the participation without a session.resume
scenarios.why: A renewed credential on the same socket keeps its connection id, so there is nothing to resume.

scenarios.title: After a drop, the next authenticated socket sends session.resume with the participation's proof, and the host reads the roster at once
scenarios.why: Events sent while the socket was down may be lost, so the host checks who is still in the session before going on.

scenarios.title: A refused session.resume ends the session with the server's code
scenarios.why: The window ended, the session closed or another socket resumed first; there is nothing left to resume.

scenarios.title: A dropped participation waits 30 seconds for a new socket, then ends without trying to resume
scenarios.why: The server holds a dropped participation for 30 seconds; after that a resume can only be refused.

scenarios.title: A close 1013 auth_unavailable resumes like a drop; a close 1008 credential_revoked ends the session as a sign-out
scenarios.why: 1013 keeps the credential, so a new socket can resume; after a 1008 the same credential is refused on every socket.

scenarios.title: A 401 on the host's roster read ends the session as a sign-out
scenarios.why: A 401 means the credential is refused, which every client treats as logout.

scenarios.title: A guest's first offer starts attempt epoch 1 at seq 1, goes out again after 1, 2 and 4 seconds without an ack, and is then abandoned
scenarios.why: The server delivers a signal at most once, so only the peer's ack says it arrived.

scenarios.title: The peer's p2p.signal.ack for the attempt and seq stops the retries
scenarios.why: Retrying a signal that arrived would only make the peer drop a duplicate.

scenarios.title: Every copy of a signal is acknowledged, and the peer transport gets it once
scenarios.why: The first ack may be the one lost, but ICE must not apply the same offer twice.

scenarios.title: The host takes an offer only above the highest epoch it accepted for that guest participation, and a rejoin starts again at epoch 1
scenarios.why: A delayed first offer must not replace the guest's newer attempt; a new participation is a new guest.

scenarios.title: A candidate and the second fragment that arrive before the first fragment are held, then the offer is handed over whole before the candidate
scenarios.why: ICE cannot take a candidate before the description it belongs to, and a description is only usable once all its parts are in.

scenarios.title: An offer too large for one signal goes out in consecutive fragments of at most 4,096 serialized bytes, and one above 32 KiB is refused without a send
scenarios.why: haiven-api refuses data above 4,096 bytes as Go serializes it, escapes included, with invalid_payload.

scenarios.title: Every 30 seconds the host reads the roster and drops any connected peer it no longer lists
scenarios.why: A lost session.member.left must not leave a removed player connected.

scenarios.title: session.member.left naming a guest drops that guest's connection on the host at once
scenarios.why: The server has removed the participation; waiting for the connection to fail or the next roster read keeps a removed player in the game.

scenarios.title: session.member.left naming the controller's own participation ends the session with the server's reason
scenarios.why: A kicked player must stop playing at once, not when the host's connection times out.

scenarios.title: session.closed ends the session with its reason, and a second one changes nothing
scenarios.why: Closing every peer connection is tied to the end of the session, which must be reported once.

scenarios.title: A relay-only ICE servers reply makes the session's ICE policy relay before the first signal
scenarios.why: Under relay-only no host or server-reflexive candidate may ever leave the device, so the policy must be set when the first connection is made.

scenarios.title: ICE servers are fetched again once refreshAfter passes, and not before
scenarios.why: TURN credentials expire during a long match; a new peer connection needs servers that are still valid.

scenarios.title: A refused ICE servers refresh keeps the old servers and is tried again 30 seconds later
scenarios.why: A connection made meanwhile still needs servers, and the next fetch may succeed.

steps.advance: The controller's clock moves forward by `seconds`.
steps.attach: A new game socket is attached to the controller as its current socket. It is not open yet.
steps.call: The game calls the controller: `create` with `maxMembers`, `join` with `sessionId` and an optional `joinCode`, `leave`, or `peerOpen`, which is the peer transport reporting the data channels to `userId` open. A create or join ends later with an `admitted` or `refused` event.
steps.close: The server closes the current socket with the WebSocket close `code` and `reason`.
steps.expectEvent: The controller has reported `event` since the previous expectEvent, with `fields` when given: admitted (sessionId, participationId, hostUserId, hosting, icePolicy), refused (error), ended (reason, code), memberLeft (userId, reason), peerDropped (userId), abandoned (to, seq), signalRefused (to, error), iceOptions (policy, servers), connectionLost, or resumed.
steps.expectQuiet: Every frame the SDK wrote, every REST request it made and every signal handed to the peer transport has been consumed by an expect step.
steps.expectRest: The next REST request the SDK made has `method` and `path`. `fields` and `capture` read its JSON body as expectSent reads a frame.
steps.expectSent: The next frame the SDK wrote has `type`. `bind` names an alias for its requestId. `fields` maps a dotted path in the frame to the value it must have; a path that steps into a string reads that string as JSON. A value {"ref": alias} must equal the bound value, {"pattern": re} must be a string matching the regular expression, and {"maxSerializedBytes": n} must be a string of at most n bytes once JSON-encoded with <, >, &, U+2028 and U+2029 escaped. `capture` maps an alias to a path whose value later steps use.
steps.expectSignal: The next signal the signaling handed to the peer transport came `from` that user with `kind`, and with `sdp` or `candidate` when given.
steps.expectState: The controller is in `state`: idle, admitting, in_session or resuming.
steps.open: The current socket becomes writable and the SDK starts its session.
steps.serve: The scripted server delivers `frame` on the current socket. Every object {"ref": alias} inside it is replaced by the value bound to that alias, and every {"secondsFromNow": n} by the ISO 8601 UTC time n seconds after the runner's wall clock.
steps.serveRest: The REST API answers the oldest unanswered request with `status` and the JSON `body`, or, when `lost` is true, the connection closes before any reply.
steps.signal: The peer transport hands the signaling a signal for `to`: `kind` offer or answer with `sdp`, or candidate with `candidate`. An `sdp` given as `sdpRepeat` and `times` is that text repeated.
